x: B is incorrect: nominated members of Parliament (and members of Legislative Councils) do not vote for the President. The electoral college is elected MPs and elected MLAs of States, Delhi and Puducherry; disputes go to the Supreme Court.
t: Remember only elected members vote for the President.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the President is only the constitutional head because real executive power lies with the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister.
t: Ask whether R is why the President is nominal.

x: Article 52 – there shall be a President; 53 – executive power vested in the President; 72 – pardons and related relief; 123 – ordinances.
t: Match each Article to the President's power.

x: I, II and IV are correct: the election is indirect, by proportional representation through the single transferable vote and secret ballot, and the Supreme Court decides disputes. III is wrong: nominated MPs do not vote.
t: Check who is excluded from the electoral college.

x: The President addresses his resignation to the Vice-President (who informs the Lok Sabha Speaker). The oath is given by the Chief Justice of India — a common distractor.
t: Separate who receives the resignation from who gives the oath.

x: C is incorrect: if both the President's and Vice-President's offices are vacant, the Chief Justice of India (or the senior-most Supreme Court judge) acts as President, not the Prime Minister.
t: Recall the line of succession for acting President.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: MLAs vote in the President's election, while only Parliament impeaches him; one fact does not explain the other.
t: Election and impeachment involve different bodies.

x: Both are true: the President's reference to the Supreme Court under Article 143 gets a non-binding opinion, and he can return a Bill (except a Money Bill) only once for reconsideration.
t: Recall the limits on advisory opinion and suspensive veto.

x: Rajendra Prasad – first President; Pratibha Patil – first woman President; Droupadi Murmu – first tribal President; the Chief Justice of India – administers the President's oath.
t: Match each person to the 'first', and the office to the oath.

x: Three: Articles 352 (National Emergency), 356 (President's Rule) and 360 (Financial Emergency) are emergency powers. Article 143 is the advisory reference to the Supreme Court.
t: Remove the non-emergency Article and count.

x: The President issues Ordinances under Article 123 only when Parliament (either House) is not in session. The other options describe conditions with no link to ordinances.
t: Link ordinances to Parliament being in recess.

x: All five are correct: the President exercises the Union's executive power directly or through subordinates, is the First Citizen, and symbolises the nation's unity, integrity and solidarity.
t: Recall how the President is described.

x: Article 53(2) vests the supreme command of the Defence Forces in the President. Being an integral part of Parliament comes from Article 79.
t: Link Article 53(2) to the defence forces.

x: Elected Lok Sabha members vote in both elections, nominated Rajya Sabha members vote only for the Vice-President, Legislative Council members vote in neither, and the Delhi and Puducherry Assemblies were added to the Presidential college by the 70th Amendment, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Compare the two electoral colleges: elected versus nominated, Parliament versus States.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I
(a) Elected members of the Lok Sabha
(b) Nominated members of the Rajya Sabha
(c) Members of State Legislative Councils
(d) Elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of Delhi and Puducherry
List-II
(i) Vote in both the Presidential and the Vice-Presidential elections
(ii) Vote in the Vice-Presidential election but not in the Presidential election
(iii) Vote in neither election
(iv) Added to the Presidential Electoral College by the 70th Amendment

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: MLA vote values ensure uniformity among States, while MP vote values ensure parity between the Union and the States — two separate principles.
t: Two rules for two sets of voters do not explain each other.

x: Under Article 58 a candidate must be an Indian citizen, have completed 35 years, be qualified to be a Lok Sabha member and hold no office of profit.
t: Match each type of condition to its rule.

x: Under Article 57 the President is eligible for re-election any number of times — unlike the US two-term limit.
t: Contrast with the US limit.

x: All four are correct: the President can be impeached for violating the Constitution under Article 61; either House can bring the charge, and each must pass it by two-thirds of its total membership.
t: Recall the ground, Article and majority for impeachment.
s:
Consider the following statements regarding the impeachment of the President:
I. The President can be removed by impeachment for violation of the Constitution.
II. Article 61 deals with the impeachment of the President.
III. Either House of Parliament can prefer a charge for impeachment.
IV. A special majority is required in both Houses of Parliament.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: The President's Succession Act, 1969 governs who acts when both the President's and Vice-President's offices are vacant.
t: Recall the 1969 succession law.

x: The President appoints as Prime Minister the leader who commands a Lok Sabha majority, appoints other Ministers on the PM's advice, appoints Governors as executive heads of States, and appoints Supreme Court judges, who retire at 65, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the feature that sets each Presidential appointee apart.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I
(a) Prime Minister
(b) Other Ministers
(c) Governors
(d) Judges of the Supreme Court
List-II
(i) Appointed as the leader commanding a majority in the Lok Sabha
(ii) Appointed on the advice of the Prime Minister
(iii) Executive head of a State
(iv) Retire on attaining 65 years of age

x: The President appoints all seven: High Court judges, the CAG, the Attorney General, the UPSC Chairman and members, Election Commissioners and Finance Commission members — each matches its own name, as in option D.
t: Look for the code that pairs each item with itself.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: appointing the majority leader as PM is a convention; Article 78's right to seek information is a separate relationship.
t: A later right does not explain an appointment convention.

x: All four are correct: the President is part of Parliament (Article 79), summons and prorogues it and dissolves the Lok Sabha, addresses it (Article 87) and assents to Bills (Article 111).
t: Recall the President's legislative roles.

x: All three are correct: the President has an absolute veto, a suspensive veto (returning a Bill once) and a pocket veto (keeping it pending).
t: Recall the three vetoes available to the President.

x: The President nominates 12 members to the Rajya Sabha from literature, science, art and social service. (The two Anglo-Indian Lok Sabha seats ended in 2020.)
t: Recall the number of Rajya Sabha nominees.

x: All four: under Article 72 the President can grant pardons, reprieves, respites and remissions, and suspend or commute sentences.
t: Recall the forms of clemency.

x: Article 56 fixes the President's term at five years. Article 57 is re-election, 61 impeachment and 65 the Vice-President acting as President.
t: Link the term of office to Article 56.

x: All four are correct: the President declares war and concludes peace on the Council of Ministers' advice and appoints Ambassadors and High Commissioners.
t: Recall the President's military and diplomatic powers.

x: Three: appointing a PM in a hung Parliament, dismissing a government that has lost majority and dissolving the Lok Sabha are situational discretion. Appointing Ambassadors is done on ministerial advice.
t: Separate discretion from advice-bound powers.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the 44th Amendment (1978) let the President send the Council's advice back once for reconsideration (after the 42nd made advice binding).
t: Check whether R is the source of the power in A.

x: Rajendra Prasad was the longest-serving President with two terms, Pratibha Patil the first woman President, Droupadi Murmu the first tribal and 15th President, and the President's emoluments are charged on the Consolidated Fund, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
t: Match each 'first' to the right person.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Dr. Rajendra Prasad
(b) Pratibha Patil
(c) Droupadi Murmu
(d) Emoluments of the President

List-II
(i) Charged on the Consolidated Fund of India
(ii) First Tribal President and 15th President
(iii) Longest-serving President; served two terms
(iv) First Woman President

x: Both are true: the President is first in the Order of Precedence and is the Head of State, while the Prime Minister heads the Government.
t: Separate Head of State from Head of Government.

x: D is incorrect: the Vice-President is removed by a Rajya Sabha resolution passed by a majority of all its then members (effective majority), agreed to by the Lok Sabha, after 14 days' notice — not a simple majority.
t: Check the majority required in the Rajya Sabha.

x: Article 63 – there shall be a Vice-President; 64 – ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha; 66 – election; 67 – term of office.
t: Recall Articles 63–67.

x: I, III and IV are correct: all MPs, elected and nominated, vote, by proportional representation through the single transferable vote and secret ballot. II is wrong: State Assemblies do not take part.
t: Compare with the President's electoral college.

x: Both are true: the Vice-President resigns to the President, and the President administers his oath.
t: Recall the Vice-President's resignation and oath.

x: Three: an Indian citizen, aged at least 35 and holding no office of profit. The fourth is wrong: a Vice-President must be qualified for the Rajya Sabha, not the Lok Sabha.
t: Rajya Sabha eligibility, because he chairs it.

x: The Vice-President can act as President for at most six months, within which a new President must be elected.
t: Recall the six-month limit.

x: Second-highest office after the President; modelled on the American Vice-President; first holder – Dr S. Radhakrishnan; eligible for re-election any number of times.
t: Match each item to the right fact.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: the Supreme Court's power to decide disputes comes from Article 71; the finality of its decision is a consequence, not the reason.
t: Finality is a result, not the source of jurisdiction.

x: All four are correct: the Vice-President can be re-elected any number of times, presides over the Rajya Sabha, has a casting vote in a tie, and does not preside while his own removal is considered.
t: Recall the Chairman's role and its limits.
s:
Consider the following statements:

I. The Vice-President is eligible for re-election any number of times.
II. The Vice-President presides over the sittings of the Rajya Sabha.
III. The Vice-President has a casting vote in case of a tie in the Rajya Sabha.
IV. The Vice-President does not preside when a resolution for his removal is under consideration.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: All five: death, resignation and removal vacate the office, while absence and illness make the President unable to act — in all these cases the Vice-President steps in.
t: Separate vacancy causes from inability causes.

x: Both are true: the Vice-President gets no salary for that office and is paid as Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, and while acting as President he draws the President's emoluments instead.
t: Remember he is paid as Chairman, not as Vice-President.
s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The Vice-President draws no separate salary as Vice-President; he is paid as ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
Statement B: When acting as President, the Vice-President is entitled to the President’s salary, allowances and privileges.

x: All three are correct: the President's electoral college is MPs and MLAs of States and UTs (Delhi, Puducherry), eligibility is linked to the Lok Sabha, and removal is by impeachment by both Houses.
t: Check each feature of the President's office.
s:
Consider the following statements:

I. The Presidential Electoral College consists of Members of Parliament and Members of the Legislative Assemblies of States and Union Territories.
II. The qualification for election as President is linked to eligibility for the Lok Sabha.
III. The President is removed by impeachment by both Houses of Parliament.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Both are true: the President is an integral part of Parliament (Article 79), whereas the Vice-President, though Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, is not a part of Parliament.
t: Separate being part of Parliament from presiding over a House.

x: Dr S. Radhakrishnan was the first Vice-President, Hamid Ansari held the office from 2007 to 2017, V. V. Giri acted as President in 1969 before winning the Presidency, and Dr Zakir Husain was the first President to die in office, giving a-ii, b-i, c-iv, d-iii.
t: Recall the distinctive record of each Vice-President.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I
(a) Dr. S. Radhakrishnan
(b) Mohammad Hamid Ansari
(c) V. V. Giri
(d) Dr. Zakir Husain
List-II
(i) Vice-President from 2007 to 2017
(ii) First Vice-President of India
(iii) First President to die in office
(iv) Acting President in 1969 before being elected President

x: A is incorrect: nominated MPs do vote in the Vice-Presidential election (they cannot in the President's). The Vice-President is elected, not appointed, and MLAs do not vote.
t: Nominated MPs vote for the Vice-President, not the President.

x: Both are true: the Vice-President is not a member of either House, and he draws no salary as Vice-President; he is paid as Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
t: Recall his non-membership and how he is paid.
s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The Vice-President is not a member of either House of Parliament.
Statement B: The Vice-President draws no salary in the capacity of Vice-President.

x: I and II are correct: an ordinance can be issued only when the legislature is in recess and the Head of State is satisfied that immediate action is needed. III is wrong: no ordinance while both Houses are sitting.
t: Two conditions: recess and urgency.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. An ordinance may be promulgated only when the Legislature is in recess.
II. The Head of State must be satisfied that circumstances exist requiring immediate action.
III. An ordinance may be promulgated during the full active session of both Houses.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: President – Article 123; Governor – Article 213; the President's ordinances cover Union and Concurrent subjects, the Governor's State and Concurrent subjects.
t: Match each authority to its Article and Lists.

x: B is incorrect: a Governor's ordinance must be approved by the State Legislature, not by the President (though some need prior Presidential instructions). A President's ordinance needs Parliament's approval.
t: Each ordinance goes back to its own legislature.

x: An ordinance has the same force, effect and limits as an Act of Parliament or the State Legislature. It is legislative, not executive, and cannot amend the Constitution.
t: Treat an ordinance as a temporary Act.

x: Within its legislative field an ordinance can amend, modify or repeal an ordinary law. It cannot amend the Constitution, override Fundamental Rights or last without legislative approval.
t: An ordinance can do what an ordinary law can.

x: Three: an ordinance can amend an ordinary Act, operate retrospectively and change taxes. It cannot amend the Constitution under Article 368.
t: Remove the constitutional amendment and count.

x: An ordinance lapses six weeks after the legislature reassembles unless approved earlier. Six months and six weeks is its maximum possible life.
t: Separate the six-week window from the maximum life.

x: I and III are correct: an ordinance must be laid before the legislature when it reassembles, and if the Houses meet on different dates the six weeks run from the later date. II contradicts III.
t: Remember the later date counts.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. An ordinance must be laid before Parliament or the State Legislature when it reassembles.
II. If the two Houses reassemble on different dates, the six-week period begins from the earlier date.
III. If the two Houses reassemble on different dates, the six-week period begins from the later date.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Maximum life = up to six months between sessions (Articles 85 and 174) + six weeks after reassembly = six months and six weeks.
t: Add the session gap to the six-week window.

x: The President or the Governor can withdraw their ordinance at any time (Article 123(2)(b) / 213(2)(b)).
t: Recall that withdrawal is open at any time.

x: The President's ordinance is under Article 123 and the Governor's under Article 213; the President's lapses six weeks after Parliament reassembles, and the Governor's must be approved by the State Legislature, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
t: Match each ordinance to its Article and rule.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
 a. President’s ordinance
 b. Governor’s ordinance
 c. President’s ordinance after reassembly
 d. Governor’s ordinance after reassembly

List-II
 i. Approval by State Legislature
 ii. Article 123
 iii. Ceases six weeks after Parliament reassembles
 iv. Article 213

Choose the correct code:

x: Both are true and R explains A: in Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) the Court held re-promulgation without legislative approval a 'fraud on the Constitution', showing ordinances are open to judicial review.
t: Check whether R is an example of A in action.

x: All three are correct: the Governor usually needs no prior Presidential instruction, but it is required in three cases — where a Bill would need prior sanction, would be reserved, or would need Presidential assent.
t: Recall the three exceptions for the Governor.
s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Governor’s ordinance-making power:
I. Prior Presidential instruction is not applicable in every case.
II. Prior Presidential instruction is mandatory in three specific cases.
III. These cases relate to a Bill requiring prior sanction, reservation, or Presidential assent.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Three are correct: the President and the Governor can each withdraw an ordinance at any time, and re-promulgation without legislative approval subverts the Constitution. Statement 3 is wrong — ordinances are subject to judicial review.
t: Spot the claim of immunity from review.

x: Both are true and R explains A: because an ordinance has the force of an Act, it can amend, modify or repeal an ordinary law within its legislative field.
t: Ask whether equal force explains the power to amend.

x: A is true: an ordinance can make or change tax provisions within legislative power. B is false: an ordinance is 'law' under Article 13(2) and is void if it abridges Fundamental Rights.
t: Fundamental Rights limit ordinances like any law.

x: Article 123 – Part V; Article 213 – Part VI; Article 85 – six-month limit between Parliament's sessions; Article 174 – the same for State Legislatures.
t: Pair the Union and State versions.

x: An ordinance can amend an ordinary Act (within competence) and have retrospective effect; it cannot abridge Fundamental Rights and cannot be issued when the legislature is in full session.
t: Separate what an ordinance can and cannot do.

x: In a bicameral legislature an ordinance cannot be issued when both Houses are in session; it is allowed if either House is not sitting.
t: Remember one House in recess is enough.

x: D.C. Wadhwa – 1987 (repeated re-promulgation in Bihar condemned); Krishna Kumar Singh – 2017; Article 13(2) – an ordinance abridging Part III is void; Article 368 – amendment power not available through an ordinance.
t: Match the cases to years and the Articles to limits.

x: In a State with one House, the Governor can issue an ordinance only when that House is not in session and he is satisfied that immediate action is needed.
t: Two conditions: recess and urgency.
